---
title: "Predictive modeling of claims status"
author: "Aashish Krishann" 
date: today
---

### Abstract

This project develops text-based models to predict the claims status of insurance-related webpages using both binary and multiclass labels. Raw HTML was processed by extracting all paragraph and header content, followed by cleaning, lemmatization, stop-word removal, tokenization, and TF-IDF feature construction. Using these features, a Random Forest classifier was trained for binary classification and achieved an estimated ~82% accuracy. A second Random Forest model was trained for the multiclass setting and achieved 80% accuracy. Both fitted models were exported along with predictions for the 929 unlabeled webpages.

### Preprocessing

We began by ingesting the raw HTML from both the labeled training set and the unlabeled test set. For each webpage, we extracted all visible textual content from paragraphs and header tags to capture both narrative and structural information. The extracted text was then cleaned by removing URLs, emails, punctuation, digits, and symbols, standardizing spacing, and converting all content to lowercase. Words were lemmatized to reduce them to their base form, and common stop-words were removed. The cleaned text was tokenized into individual word tokens, after which we computed TF-IDF scores for each token and retained the top 100 highest-TF-IDF terms per document to reduce dimensionality while preserving informative features. These token-level features were then expanded into a sparse document-term matrix and aligned across training and test sets to ensure a consistent feature space for modeling.

### Methods

For the predictive modeling tasks, we trained separate models for the binary and multiclass classification problems. In both cases, the TF-IDF document-term matrix served as the feature set, restricted to the top terms per document to reduce sparsity and improve computational efficiency.

# Binary Classification.
To predict the open/closed claim status, we fit a Random Forest classifier using all TF-IDF features. The model was trained with 500 trees and an mtry parameter set to the square root of the number of features, which is standard for high-dimensional text data. The Random Forest framework was chosen for its robustness to noisy features and its strong performance on sparse inputs without the need for extensive hyperparameter tuning. The model was trained on the full training set, and performance was evaluated using out-of-bag error as well as a separate holdout validation split.

# Multiclass Classification.
For the multiclass setting, we used an identical modeling framework and feature construction process. A second Random Forest classifier was trained with the same hyperparameter configuration (500 trees and mtry = sqrt(p)). This choice ensured methodological consistency across tasks and allowed the model to capture nonlinear interactions among high-dimensional text features. Performance was again assessed using out-of-bag estimates alongside an 80/20 validation split to confirm model stability.

In both cases, the final fitted models were saved as deployable .rds files, and predictions for the unlabeled test set were generated in the required format.

### Results

# Binary Classification

The Random Forest model for the binary task (open vs. closed claims) achieved strong predictive performance. Overall accuracy was 0.80, indicating that the model correctly classified 80% of the webpages. Sensitivity and specificity were well-balanced, showing that the model performs similarly for both open and closed claim categories.

Table 1. Binary Classification Performance

Metric	Value
Sensitivity	0.79
Specificity	0.81
Accuracy	0.80


# Multiclass Classification

For the multiclass task, predicting detailed claim categories, the model also achieved an overall accuracy of 0.80. Macro-averaged sensitivity and specificity were 0.78 and 0.82, re spectively, summarizing performance across all classes. This demonstrates that the model generalizes well even in a more complex prediction setting.

Sensitivity	0.78
